newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Menem accepts minister's resignation.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Menem accepts minister's resignation.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem on Thursday accepted the resignation of his justice minister, who admitted to contacts with a tycoon suspected in a murder case and alleged to be a mobster.
Presidential spokesman Raul Delgado told reporters in a terse statement that Elias Jassan would be replaced as minister by Ambassador to Washington Raul Granillo Ocampo.

The Peronist president, fresh from attending the U.N. environmental conference in New York, received Jassan in the weekly Cabinet meeting and decided it was best that the scandal-tainted official distance himself from the government.
The private news agency DyN quoted Jassan as telling photographers as he entered the meeting: "Go ahead boys, these (photos) will be the last."

Jassan, Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Menem's Chief of Staff Alberto Kohan have been accused by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo of manipulating judges to protect tycoon Alfredo Yabran's alleged criminal activities. Cavallo accuses Yabran of being the "head of the mafia."

The officials all denied the charges and Yabran says he has done no wrong. But Jassan was caught lying a week ago when he first denied he knew Yabran, then had to admit to receiving more than 100 phone calls from the businessman's office.

Police also say Yabran is their "only lead" in investigating who ordered the murder of photographer Jose Luis Cabezas in January. Cabezas, who took photos of Yabran for Noticias magazine, was shot and his body burned.

The scandal comes four months before key midterm elections as the administration struggles to cope with social unrest, internal party divisions and low levels of public support. After being re-elected with 50 percent of the vote in 1995, Menem barely garners even double-digit approval in some polls.

Protesters angered by high unemployment have blocked roads with burning tires in more than a dozen provinces in recent weeks. Joblessness nationally is 17.3 percent but it rises to as high as 40 percent in more hard-pressed areas.

The protests and scandal have enabled the centre-left Frepaso alliance to trim the Peronist lead to between two to five points ahead of October's congressional election. The opposition insisted Jassan's resignation would not stop its probes into Yabran's activities and ties with the government.

"The government is trying to assume the least political risk," said Juan Pablo Cafiero, a Frepaso member of the congressional anti-mafia committee. "We will have to determine if there was an illicit relationship between Yabran and some members of government."

Sen. Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner, who was ejected from the Peronist Party last month for rebelling against the party line, called for more Cabinet changes, charging that almost all ministers have "lost credibility."
Granillo Ocampo will be replaced in Washington by Argentina's ambassador to Brazil, Diego Guelar.
